more.d: Jawbone from Peștera cu Oase, Romania, about 40,000 years old; its DNA shows a recent Neanderthal ancestor.
Juvenile modern-human skeleton from a rock shelter near Beirut, dated about 40,800–39,200 years ago.
Good evidence of people in the Japanese archipelago from about 36,000 BC, long before pottery.
Modern-human skull from Niah Caves, Borneo, dated to about 37,000 years ago.
From about 33,000 years ago the Gravettian spread across Europe: mammoth hunters known for Venus figurines and rich burials.
Dog-like canid skull from Goyet Caves, Belgium, dated about 31,700 years old; possibly an early, failed domestication.
Painted stone slabs from Apollo 11 Cave, Namibia, about 30,000 years old: among Africa's oldest figurative art.
First phase of art in Cosquer Cave, Marseille, about 27,000 years ago; its entrance is now 37 m under the sea.
Stones from a Mexican high-altitude cave dated to about 26,000 years ago; whether they are human tools is debated.

know.d: Neanderthals vanished around 40,000 years ago, a few thousand years after modern humans reached Europe. Interbreeding means most non-Africans carry some Neanderthal DNA.
Swabian Jura caves produced the Lion-man, the Venus of Hohle Fels and bone flutes, about 40,000 years old: the oldest known sculpture and instruments.
Charcoal paintings of lions, rhinos and horses made about 36,000 years ago show fully developed artistic skill early in the Upper Paleolithic.

know.t: Humans reach the edges of the world
know.d: By this era modern humans lived in Australia (Lake Mungo) and above the Arctic Circle (Yana), adapting to deserts and tundra.
The Campanian Ignimbrite super-eruption near Naples and the Laschamp geomagnetic excursion hit Europe around the time Neanderthals declined.
Small female figures like the Venus of Willendorf and the fired-clay Venus of Dolní Věstonice were made across Europe from about 30,000 years ago.

papers.t: A Draft Sequence of the Neandertal Genome
papers.why: First Neanderthal genome; showed Neanderthals contributed DNA to non-African modern humans.

papers.t: The genetic history of Ice Age Europe
papers.why: Genomes of 51 Ice Age Europeans reveal population turnovers between 45,000 and 7,000 years ago.

papers.t: The timing and spatiotemporal patterning of Neanderthal disappearance
papers.why: Radiocarbon dating of 40 sites places Neanderthal disappearance at about 41,000–39,000 years ago.

papers.t: An early modern human from Romania with a recent Neanderthal ancestor
papers.why: Oase 1 had a Neanderthal ancestor only 4–6 generations back.

papers.t: New ages for human occupation and climatic change at Lake Mungo, Australia
papers.why: Dated Mungo Man and Australian occupation to about 40,000 years ago.

papers.t: New flutes document the earliest musical tradition in southwestern Germany
papers.why: Bone and ivory flutes from Hohle Fels are the oldest known musical instruments.

papers.t: A female figurine from the basal Aurignacian of Hohle Fels Cave in southwestern Germany
papers.why: Announced the Venus of Hohle Fels, the oldest known depiction of a human.

papers.why: Linked the Laschamps geomagnetic excursion to climate and environmental change using a New Zealand kauri tree record.

more.d: Taupō volcano in New Zealand produced the Oruanui eruption about 25,700 years ago, forming the caldera now filled by Lake Taupō.
Ivory head from Brassempouy, France, about 25,000 years old: one of the earliest realistic human faces.
Painted 'dappled horses' in Pech Merle cave, France, about 25,000 years old.
North African microlithic culture appears around 25,000–23,000 years ago and lasts until the early Holocene.
Mal'ta–Buret' culture near Lake Baikal, about 24,000 years ago; the Mal'ta boy's genome links Siberians and Native Americans.
Cut-marked bones from Yukon caves dated about 24,000 years ago may show people in Beringia during the LGM.
Levantine hunter-gatherers with microlith tools, about 23,000–15,000 years ago; ancestors of the Natufians.
The Solutrean industry of France and Iberia, about 22,000–17,000 years ago, made thin, finely flaked stone points.
Notched baboon bone from Ishango, Congo, about 20,000 years old, sometimes read as an early counting tool.
Late Paleolithic Nile camps near Aswan, about 19,000–17,000 years ago, rich in plant-food and fish remains.

know.d: Ice sheets reached their greatest extent about 26,000–20,000 years ago, and sea level was about 125 m lower than today.
Low sea levels exposed Beringia, linking Siberia and Alaska; people may have waited there before moving south.
Hunter-gatherers in southern China made pottery about 20,000 years ago, more than 10,000 years before agriculture.
Lascaux's painted horses, aurochs and deer, about 17,000–22,000 years old, are among the most famous artworks of the Ice Age.
Brush huts on the Sea of Galilee, about 23,000 years old, preserve wild barley and wheat: an early step toward farming.
Human footprints at White Sands have been dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, though the dating is debated.

papers.why: Dated when each ice sheet reached its maximum (about 26,500–19,000 years ago) and when retreat began.

papers.t: Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene
papers.why: Reconstructed sea level from about 35,000 years ago to the present, including the LGM lowstand.

papers.why: The ICE-6G_C model of global ice-sheet thickness and topography since the LGM.

papers.why: The 24,000-year-old Mal'ta boy genome shows Native Americans descend partly from ancient North Eurasians.

papers.t: Constraints on the magnitude and patterns of ocean cooling at the Last Glacial Maximum
papers.why: Global synthesis of sea-surface temperatures during the LGM.

papers.t: Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China
papers.why: Dated the world's oldest known pottery to 20,000–19,000 years ago.

papers.why: Ohalo II plant remains show hunter-gatherers using wild cereals and many small seeds 23,000 years ago.

papers.t: Evidence of humans in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum
papers.why: Dated the White Sands footprints to about 23,000–21,000 years ago.

more.d: Pottery from Yuchanyan Cave, Hunan, about 18,300–15,430 years old, among the oldest known.
Unusual human fossils from Yunnan and Guangxi, about 17,800–11,500 years old; their classification is debated.
Reindeer hunters recolonise northern Europe about 15,500–13,100 years ago as the ice retreats.
A Southern Hemisphere cooling about 14,700–13,000 years ago interrupted the deglacial warming.
Florida sinkhole site with stone tools and a butchered mastodon about 14,550 years ago, before Clovis.
Human coprolites from Oregon dated about 14,300 years ago, early evidence of people in North America.
At the Natufian village of Ain Mallaha (Eynan), a woman was buried with her hand on a puppy.
Euphrates village where rye may have been cultivated from the start of the Younger Dryas.
Younger Dryas reindeer hunters of northern Europe using bow and arrow, 12,900–11,700 years ago.
The Folsom tradition followed Clovis on the Great Plains about 10,800–10,200 BCE, hunting extinct bison.

know.d: The world warmed suddenly in the Bølling–Allerød, then plunged back into cold in the Younger Dryas before the Holocene began about 11,700 years ago.
Melting ice raised sea level by about 16–25 m in a few centuries during Meltwater pulse 1A.
Natufian hunter-gatherers in the Levant built permanent stone houses and cemeteries before farming.
Monte Verde in Chile and Clovis sites in North America show humans across the Americas by about 14,500–13,000 years ago.
Mammoths, woolly rhinos and many American large mammals disappeared as climate changed and humans spread.
The Bonn–Oberkassel dog, buried with two people about 14,000 years ago, is one of the earliest certain domestic dogs.

papers.t: Global warming preceded by increasing carbon dioxide concentrations during the last deglaciation
papers.why: Global temperature stack shows CO2 rise led most of the deglacial warming.

papers.t: Assessing the Causes of Late Pleistocene Extinctions on the Continents
papers.why: Concluded both humans and climate drove the megafaunal extinctions.

papers.t: The Younger Dryas cold interval as viewed from central Greenland
papers.why: Greenland ice cores show the Younger Dryas began and ended within decades.

papers.t: Monte Verde: Seaweed, Food, Medicine, and the Peopling of South America
papers.why: Dated seaweed at Monte Verde to about 14,000 years ago, confirming pre-Clovis occupation.

papers.t: Global climate evolution during the last deglaciation
papers.why: Synthesis of the sequence of deglacial climate events across both hemispheres.

papers.t: Redefining the Age of Clovis: Implications for the Peopling of the Americas
papers.why: Shortened the Clovis period to about 13,100–12,800 years ago.

papers.t: The genome of a Late Pleistocene human from a Clovis burial site in western Montana
papers.why: The Anzick child genome shows Clovis people were ancestral to many Native Americans.

papers.t: The Natufian culture in the Levant, threshold to the origins of agriculture
papers.why: Classic synthesis of Natufian sedentism as the prelude to farming.

Giant wooden figure from a Urals peat bog, carved about 11,500 years ago according to later dating.
Naturally mummified man from Nevada, about 11,500 years old; repatriated to the Fallon Paiute-Shoshone Tribe in 2016.
Seedless figs from Gilgal I, about 11,400 years old, suggest fig trees were grown from cuttings.
Pottery from Ounjougou, Mali, made before 9400 BCE, the earliest found in Africa.
Mesolithic lakeside site in Yorkshire occupied about 9300–8500 BC, with a preserved timber structure.
The oldest known settlement in Estonia, on the Pärnu River, about 9000 cal BC.
Village in southeast Turkey founded about 8630 BC; possibly where pigs were first domesticated.
Taurine cattle were domesticated from wild aurochs about 10,500 years ago in Anatolia, the Levant and western Iran.
Pre-Pottery Neolithic B settlement near Urfa, 8400–8100 BC, related to the Göbekli Tepe tradition.
Mesolithic skeleton from Gough's Cave in Cheddar Gorge, England, directly radiocarbon dated to about 8300 BC.

know.d: Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe, with carved T-shaped pillars, were built by people who still mostly hunted and gathered.
Einkorn, emmer, barley, lentils, peas, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent.
Sheep, goats, pigs and cattle became the first livestock in the Near East about 11,000–10,000 years ago.
A stone tower was built at Jericho around 8000 BC in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, one of the oldest known stone monuments.
During the African humid period the Sahara had grasslands, trees and lakes that supported people and animals.

papers.why: Showed how people moved into and out of the Sahara as the African humid period began and ended.

papers.why: Ganj Dareh bones show goat herding in Iran by 10,000 years ago.

papers.why: Review of how farming emerged gradually across the Fertile Crescent.

papers.why: Evidence of large-scale feasting and cereal processing at Göbekli Tepe.

papers.why: Chogha Golan shows plant cultivation in the eastern Fertile Crescent from about 11,700 years ago.

A grave at Shillourokambos, Cyprus, about 9,500 years old, holds a person and a cat side by side.
Hand stencils and hunting scenes in Patagonia, painted in waves from about 7300 BC.
Early farming village in the Zagros foothills of Iraq, oldest levels about 7090 BC.
Drainage ditches in the New Guinea highlands about 9,000 years ago mark independent early agriculture.
Village in Henan with crane-bone flutes, early rice, fermented drink and possible proto-writing signs, from about 7000 BC.
Danube Gorges settlement with trapezoidal buildings and stone sculptures from about 7000 BC.
Skeleton from the Columbia River, Washington, dated about 8,400–8,690 calibrated years BP.
Early farming culture of the Balkans, about 6200–4500 BCE.
Rising seas flooded the Bassian Plain about 8,000 years ago, forming Bass Strait and isolating Tasmania.

know.t: Farming begins independently in many places
know.d: Rice in the Yangtze valley, squash and maize in Mexico, and crops in New Guinea were domesticated separately from the Near East.
One of the largest early farming settlements, in central Anatolia, built around 7100 BC and occupied until about 5600 BC.
Farmers from Anatolia reached Greece about 7000–6500 BC and carried agriculture into the Balkans.
Drainage of glacial Lake Agassiz cooled the North Atlantic for one to two centuries around 6200 BC.
Doggerland, the plain linking Britain and Europe, was cut off by rising seas, perhaps finished by the Storegga tsunami about 6200 BCE.
At Nataruk in Kenya, a group of hunter-gatherers was killed with arrows and clubs about 10,000 years ago.

more.d: Ryan and Pitman proposed that the Mediterranean abruptly flooded the Black Sea basin about 7,600 years ago; the idea remains debated.
The Faiyum A industry is the earliest farming culture in the Nile Valley, dated to about 5600–4400 BC.
One of the earliest rice-cultivating cultures, in the lower Yangtze; Tianluoshan shows rice becoming domesticated.
Eridu in southern Mesopotamia, long regarded as the oldest Sumerian city, was founded around 5400 BC in the early Ubaid period.
Chinchorro fishers of the Atacama coast began artificially mummifying their dead by about 5050 BCE, millennia before Egypt.
A circular ditch-and-palisade enclosure in Germany, built about 4900 BC and aligned to the winter solstice sunrise and sunset.
One of Europe's oldest megalithic monuments, a long chambered cairn in Brittany begun about 4850 BC.
A Yangshao-culture farming village near Xi'an with round houses and painted pottery, occupied about 4700–3600 BC.
The Hongshan culture of northeast China produced some of the earliest carved jades, including 'pig dragons'.
Thousands of standing stones in rows in Brittany; some may date to as early as 4500 BC.
Susa in southwest Iran was founded around 4200 BC and later became a capital of Elam and Persia.

know.d: Linear Pottery (LBK) farmers spread across central Europe from about 5500 BC, living in timber longhouses and bringing crops and livestock.
Copper was smelted in the Balkans by around 5000 BC, starting the metal age of human technology.
The Varna cemetery (c. 4600–4300 BC) holds the oldest worked-gold treasure, showing strong social inequality.
Mass graves at Talheim and Schletz show whole communities killed around 5000 BC.
Ubaid villages in southern Mesopotamia used irrigation and built temples, laying foundations for later cities.
During the African humid period the Sahara had lakes and grassland where herders built sites like Nabta Playa.

papers.why: Farming triggered a worldwide rise in birth rates and population.

North Caucasus culture whose royal kurgan held thousands of gold and silver objects.
Megalithic temples on Gozo, Malta, built about 3600 BC, among the oldest free-standing buildings.
A 5,500-year-old leather shoe preserved in the Areni-1 cave in Armenia.
On the Ecuadorian coast, the Valdivia culture made some of the earliest pottery in the Americas.
An abrupt cold, wet climate swing around 5,500 years ago, recorded in Alpine and other archives.
Jade-working society in the Yangtze delta (3300–2300 BC) with a walled city and water works, possibly an early state.
A stone-built Neolithic village in Orkney, with stone furniture, occupied about 3180–2500 BC.
A great passage tomb in Ireland built about 3100 BC, whose passage catches the midwinter sunrise.
Carved slate palette from Hierakonpolis showing King Narmer, linked to Egypt's unification.
Around 3100 BC Uruk may have housed up to 50,000 people, the largest city in the world.

know.d: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew into a true city with temples, administrators and specialists.
Cuneiform in Mesopotamia and hieroglyphs in Egypt emerged from accounting and labels between 3400 and 3100 BC.
Wheeled vehicles appear around 3500 BC from Europe to Mesopotamia; the Ljubljana Marshes wheel is the oldest surviving one.
Around 3150 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were united under rulers like Narmer.
The African humid period ended roughly 6,000–5,000 years ago, turning grassland into desert and pushing people to the Nile.
Ötzi, who died in the Alps around 3230 BC, preserves clothing, tools, a copper axe and his genome.

Central and northern European culture with strong Yamnaya-related ancestry, from about 2900 BC.

Egypt's first pyramid, built for King Djoser at Saqqara in the 27th century BC.

Microblade-using people spread from Alaska to become the first inhabitants of Arctic Canada and Greenland.

Southern Urals culture with the earliest known spoked-wheel chariots, about 2200–1900 BC.

Egypt built the Step Pyramid and then the Great Pyramid of Giza, the largest pyramid ever, around 2600 BC.
Planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa flourished in the Indus Valley from about 2600 BC.
Sargon of Akkad united Mesopotamian city-states into the Akkadian Empire around 2334 BC.
Caral in Peru had monumental pyramids by about 2600 BC, contemporary with Egypt's.
